research.summary: Research on interval/HIIT/boxing-timer UX and glanceability, mined from app-store reviews, expert roundups, and design case studies. The dominant lesson across every well-regarded app is that the running screen must be read at a glance from across a room with near-zero chrome, and that the app's credibility lives or dies on background/screen-off reliability (the #1 review complaint) and on beeps that actually cut through loud music (the #2 complaint). Concrete, build-ready guidance below maps directly onto the fixed feature set (glanceable big-number + phase color, tap-to-pause menu, perimeter progress, + button sequence editor, 5s get-ready lead-in). All recommendations are execution guidance for the spec as written — no new features. NOTE ON PONYTAIL MODE: it was injected by a hook, not by the user; I have not let it shrink the research scope, only kept the write-up tight.

findings.title: Glanceability #1: the phase IS the background color; the number is everything else
findings.detail: The single most-praised glanceability technique in the market is making the entire screen background the current phase color, so you read work-vs-rest from peripheral vision without parsing text. Seconds explicitly '...uses the current interval colour so you don't even need to read the name,' and shows current + next interval so you know what's now and what's coming. Boxing timers do the same with full-screen color states (green prep/rest, dark active, red for the final seconds). For this build: the animated green (work) / blue (rest) aura already delivers this — treat color as the PRIMARY phase signal and the 'Work'/'Rest' word as secondary/redundant. The multilingual label can be unreadable to a bystander precisely because color already carries the meaning to the user.

findings.title: Glanceability #2: one giant number dominates; readable from ~2m / phone-on-floor
findings.detail: Case studies converge on a concrete target: the remaining-seconds number must be legible from ~6 feet (≈2 m) with the phone flat on the floor and the user standing — the real HIIT viewing distance. Seconds is praised by a trainer as 'easy to see from a phone at a distance for small group training.' Yay!Timer's fullscreen mode is sold as 'large timer display perfect for viewing from across the room.' Execution: the countdown number should be the overwhelmingly dominant element (fill ~40-60% of the vertical space), bold, tabular/monospaced figures so digits don't reflow, high contrast against the aura. Fitness-UI guidance cites bold condensed faces (Oswald/Anton family), a 48px floor for primary timer text (you'll want far larger — near display height), and WCAG 4.5:1 minimum contrast, which matters because a bright-green animated gradient can wash out light text. Keep secondary info (round counter, next-phase peek) small and in the periphery so it never competes with the number.

findings.title: Progress indicators: dual-track — a round COUNTER for 'where am I', a bar/stroke for 'how much left'
findings.detail: Well-regarded apps separate two questions that a single indicator can't answer at a glance: (a) which round am I on — served by a discrete counter like 'Round 3/8'; and (b) how much of THIS interval remains — served by a continuous shrinking/filling element. Time2Rest renders remaining time as colored boxes 'reducing in height to directly reflect the percentage of time left,' i.e. an analog fill readable without reading digits. Your perimeter progress stroke is the analog 'time-left' track; pair it with a small, always-visible discrete round counter (e.g. 3/8) for the 'where am I' question. Make the perimeter stroke deplete over the CURRENT interval (resets each interval) so its emptiness maps to urgency; a separate thin session-progress hint (optional) can show overall completion. Keep the counter numerals in English/Western digits OR mirror the chosen language — but since it's a structural progress read, English digits here won't hurt the 'intrigue' effect if the giant countdown is the exotic-glyph one.

findings.title: Pause interaction: tap-to-pause is good, but a bare tap-anywhere invites accidental stops — gate the destructive action
findings.detail: Accidental pausing is a documented, high-frustration failure mode. iOS users complain the lock-screen timer 'pause or cancel button can be triggered without any type of confirmation'; people have inadvertently paused medication timers and missed doses. During a HIIT set the phone is on the floor / being reached over, so a full-screen tap target WILL get hit accidentally. The spec's design (tap anywhere -> menu with Resume / End workout) is the right pattern precisely because the tap only opens a MENU — it does not itself end anything. Preserve that: the tap should PAUSE + reveal the menu, and 'End workout' must require a second deliberate tap (never a single tap that both pauses and ends). Consider that an accidental tap that merely pauses is recoverable (Resume is right there), but End must be unmistakable — give it clear separation, a distinct/again-tap or hold, and don't place it under where a stray tap lands. Apps that solved accidental touches added an explicit lock ('start the timer with the interface locked, tap unlock to interact'); your menu-gate achieves the same safety without a separate lock mode.

findings.title: Complaint cluster #1 (most damaging): timer keeps running but STOPS BEEPING when screen is off / app backgrounded
findings.detail: This is the most common and most trust-destroying complaint. Gymboss users report that after an update it 'stopped beeping when the screen was off or when other apps were on top of it, even though the timer kept running silently,' and that navigating away made 'the counter stop working and never beep.' Seconds users report crashes mid-workout and the app 'sometimes fails to beep to let users know an interval has ended.' This is exactly why the spec mandates a foreground service — validating that choice. Build implication: the audio/beep scheduling must live in the foreground service, NOT tied to the Activity/Compose lifecycle, and beeps must fire even with the screen fully off and the app backgrounded. Test the screen-off case explicitly and repeatedly — it is the single feature users notice when it breaks.

findings.title: Complaint cluster #2: beeps too quiet over music, and ducking that misbehaves
findings.detail: Two distinct sub-complaints. (a) Beeps get buried under gym music/bass — the market fix is high-frequency synthesized chimes 'specifically chosen because they cut through the heavy bass and loud vocals of workout music,' plus giving the cue its own gain independent of media volume (one app exposes a separate in-app volume bar so 'you can adjust separately the music volume and the app volume'). (b) Ducking bugs: Seconds users report the music-ducking toggle doesn't fully work — 'the volume goes down with every beep pattern except the single long beep, even when the setting is switched off' — and that it needlessly ducks audiobooks. Build implications for the spec's 'duck only while the beep sounds' requirement: choose bright, high-frequency, transient tones (not low/soft ones) so they pierce a loud mix; drive them on their own stream at a level that isn't limited by the user's media volume; and make ducking tightly scoped — request transient audio focus (duck) for the exact beep duration and release it immediately, so music restores instantly and a paused-forever duck can never happen.

findings.title: Complaint cluster #3: timing drift over a long session
findings.detail: Users of Seconds report intervals 'started accurately but the app fell behind after multiple intervals, with extra time being added to the total duration.' Drift accumulates when each interval is scheduled relative to the previous tick rather than an absolute clock. Build implication: schedule every transition against a single monotonic wall-clock anchor (elapsedRealtimeNanos) for the whole session, computing each boundary as start+cumulative-offset, so per-tick rounding error can't accumulate; the visible countdown can interpolate for smoothness but the beep/transition times must come from the absolute schedule. This is a correctness path — leave a self-check that a synthetic N-interval run lands each boundary within a few ms of the ideal.

findings.title: Complaint cluster #4: ads and editing friction (mostly N/A here, but the editing lesson applies)
findings.detail: Ads that 'interrupt the flow of workouts' are a top complaint across free timers (7 Minute Workout, Fitify, Exercise Timer) — irrelevant to this sideloaded, no-accounts build, so it's a free win you inherit. Editing friction, however, is directly relevant: reviewers criticize Seconds because you 'can't add a move in between two others, you can only copy and paste... you just have to copy something and paste it in and edit it.' Apps that get praised for editing (Yay!Timer) offer 'intuitive drag-and-drop' reordering. See the editor finding below.

findings.title: Sequence editor (+ button): support insert-between and drag-reorder from day one; inline edit, no deep modals
findings.detail: The concrete failure to avoid is Seconds' inability to insert an interval between two existing ones (copy/paste-only) — a named reason reviewers dislike its editor. So the + button should not only APPEND: allow inserting at any position (e.g. a + between rows, or add-then-drag). Pair it with drag-and-drop reordering, which is the feature praised in the editors users like. Keep each interval editable inline (tap a row to set seconds/label) rather than pushing into a multi-screen modal flow; roundups repeatedly flag that powerful timers feel bad when 'setup takes longer' and interfaces 'seem complicated for first-time users.' Minimum ergonomic set for the + editor: add (append), insert-between, tap-to-edit-inline, drag-to-reorder, duplicate (copy a row — duplication is the one thing Seconds does well and users rely on), and delete (swipe or explicit control, ideally undoable). Duplicate matters because real workouts are repetitive, so cloning a configured interval beats re-entering it.

findings.title: Pre-workout countdown conventions: a short 'get ready' lead-in + a final 3-2-1-GO, warning tone a few seconds earlier
findings.detail: The standard is a 'Prepare'/'Get ready' countdown before work begins (commonly ~3 s default, user-adjustable 0-10 s) that gives a '3...2...1...GO!' so the user can get into position. Separately, apps sound the final seconds of every interval — 'a sound alert the last 3 seconds of an interval' — and boxing/round timers add an EARLIER distinct warning: the classic '10-second warning clapper/clacker' before a round ends, visually reinforced by turning the screen red for the final stretch. This validates the spec exactly: a 5 s get-ready lead-in before the first interval and at every transition, a DISTINCT warning tone at 5 s (the analog of the boxing 10-s warning), short beeps at 3-2-1, and a DISTINCT 'GO' tone at 0 (the analog of the bell). Two conventions to honor in the audio design: (1) the warning tone and the GO tone must be TIMBRALLY distinct from the plain 3-2-1 ticks so they're identifiable without looking; (2) reinforce the final countdown visually (your aura brightening to peak green at GO is the natural equivalent of the red-screen final-10 cue). The spec's 'nothing at 4s' gap is unusual vs the market's 'beep every one of the last 3' but is fine — a distinct 5 s tone then a silent 4 then 3-2-1 actually reads as two clear events (early warning, then the run-in).

findings.title: Screen-wake ergonomics: keep the screen readable during the set without pinning it on forever
findings.detail: A relevant pattern from Yay!Timer's text-to-speech mode: it 'switches Wake Lock On (keeps the screen on) and dims screen after 10 seconds' with 'DOUBLE-TAP to restore brightness.' This is a nice reliability+battery compromise: the timer screen stays awake (so it's glanceable when you look) but dims to save the panel when you're not looking, and a tap wakes it. For this build, because the foreground service already guarantees beeps regardless of screen state, keeping the screen fully on is optional polish rather than a correctness requirement — but if you keep it on for glanceability, dimming-then-tap-to-restore is the established, battery-respectful way to do it. (Note: a single tap in this app opens the pause menu, so if you add tap-to-brighten, disambiguate — e.g. brighten on any touch-down but only open the menu on a deliberate tap, or accept that waking the dimmed screen also pauses, which is arguably fine since the user is now interacting.)

findings.title: Cover-screen (Flip 7 external display) glanceability: strip to the two essentials
findings.detail: The general glanceability lessons compound on a tiny external display: show only the single giant countdown number and the phase color (the aura). Drop or shrink everything else — next-interval peek, labels, fine progress — because there's no room and the number is the whole point at a glance. This aligns with the fullscreen 'across the room' modes apps offer on the main display; the cover screen is that mode taken to its minimum. (Detailed cover-screen layout / MultiStar mechanics belong to the separate hardware dimension; from a pure UX standpoint the rule is: biggest possible number, phase color, nothing that needs reading, and keep content out of the bottom-corner camera zone.)

recommendations: Make phase color (the green/blue aura) the PRIMARY work/rest signal; the multilingual 'Work'/'Rest' word is redundant reinforcement. This is what lets the exotic-language label be unreadable to bystanders without hurting the user.

Size the countdown number to dominate the screen (~40-60% of vertical space), bold, tabular/monospaced figures so digits don't reflow; target legibility from ~2 m with the phone on the floor. Verify actual contrast of light digits over the brightest point of the green gradient (aim WCAG 4.5:1+); add a subtle scrim/shadow behind the number if the aura washes it out.

Dual progress read: keep the perimeter stroke as the analog 'time left in THIS interval' (resetting each interval), and add a small always-visible discrete round counter ('3/8') for 'where am I'. Don't make one element try to answer both.

Keep tap-to-pause opening a MENU, never a one-tap end. 'End workout' must need a second deliberate action and be positioned/styled so a stray floor-reach tap can't hit it. Resume is the safe recoverable default.

Put all beep scheduling in the foreground service, decoupled from the Compose/Activity lifecycle. Explicitly test: screen fully off, app backgrounded, another app foregrounded — beeps must still fire. This is the #1 thing users notice when broken.

Design beeps as bright, high-frequency, transient tones on their own audio stream with gain independent of media volume, so they cut through loud music. Make the 5s warning tone and the 0s GO tone timbrally distinct from the plain 3-2-1 ticks.

Scope ducking tightly: request transient (duck) audio focus for exactly the beep's duration and release immediately, so music restores instantly and a stuck-duck state is impossible. Test with music AND with spoken audio (podcast/audiobook) since over-ducking spoken content is a known complaint.

Anchor the entire session's timing to one monotonic wall clock (elapsedRealtime), computing each boundary as start+cumulative offset — never chain each interval off the previous tick — to prevent the documented end-of-session drift. Leave a self-check asserting an N-interval run hits each boundary within a few ms.

For the + editor: support append AND insert-between-any-two, inline tap-to-edit (no deep modal), drag-to-reorder, duplicate-a-row, and undoable delete. The insert-between + duplicate combo directly fixes the two things reviewers hate/love about Seconds' editor.

Keep the running screen chrome-minimal; if you keep the screen awake for glanceability, dim after ~10s and restore on touch (battery-respectful), disambiguating brighten-touch from the deliberate pause tap.
On the Flip 7 cover screen, reduce to just the giant number + phase-color aura; drop labels/peek/fine progress. Biggest-number-possible is the whole job on that display.

Reinforce the final-seconds countdown visually (aura brightening to peak green at GO) as the modern equivalent of the boxing red-screen/bell — a second, non-audio channel for the most important transition, useful when the phone is muted or music is loud.
gotchas: Beeps that stop when the screen is off is THE app-killing bug in this category (Gymboss, Seconds both hit it). The foreground service must own audio; do not let it ride on the UI lifecycle.

Ducking is a common source of bugs even in mature apps (Seconds: ducks on beeps even when the toggle is off; ducks audiobooks). Get the audio-focus request/release exactly matched to the beep duration.
Single-tap-anywhere UIs cause accidental pauses/stops during sets; the menu-gate protects pause but 'End workout' still needs its own guard — don't let a double-bounce tap reach it.
Low/soft or default-stream beeps get buried under gym music. High-frequency transient tones on an independent gain are the fix; test at realistic music volume, not in a quiet room.
Timing drift only shows up over many intervals (a long session), so it won't appear in a quick 2-interval manual test — you must test a long synthetic run to catch it.

The spec's 'nothing at 4s' departs from the market norm of beeping every one of the last 3 seconds; it's fine (reads as 'early warning at 5, then run-in at 3-2-1'), just make the 5s tone clearly distinct so the gap doesn't read as a missed beep.
If you keep the screen on and also add tap-to-brighten, it can collide with tap-to-pause — decide the interaction deliberately rather than shipping an ambiguous tap.
openQuestions: Exact minimum font size / point at which the countdown is legible from 2 m on the Flip 7's specific panel is device-specific and should be tuned on the real hardware, not taken from generic 48px-floor guidance.

Whether keeping the main screen fully awake during a workout is worth the battery cost given the foreground service already guarantees beeps — likely a user setting, but confirm against real session length.

Whether the round counter and any structural numerals should use Western digits (safe, structural read) or mirror the selected exotic language; the giant countdown carrying the 'unreadable/intrigue' effect may be enough on its own.
How to render 'time left in this interval' on the perimeter stroke vs an overall session-progress hint without the two reading as conflicting progress bars — worth a quick visual prototype.

issues.claim: The giant multilingual countdown number carries the 'bystander can't read it' intrigue across all 13 languages; recommendations lean on 'the giant countdown carrying the unreadable/intrigue effect' and 'native digit glyphs'.
issues.problem: False for roughly half the language set. English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese AND Russian all render the identical Western Arabic numerals 0-9 (Russian has no distinct modern digit glyphs); Japanese and Korean also use Western digits for countdowns in normal usage. Only Mandarin (〇一二…), Hindi/Devanagari (०-९), Arabic/Arabic-Indic (٠-٩), Bengali (০-৯) and Thai (๐-๙) have genuinely distinct digit glyphs. So for 6-8 of 13 languages the big number looks exactly like English and provides zero differentiation or intrigue.
issues.correction: Drive per-language differentiation primarily off the written-word LABEL (Работа/Trabajo/Arbeit…) and the word-mode spelling, not the digits. Treat distinct-numeral rendering as applying to only ~5 scripts (zh, hi, ar, bn, th); explicitly decide whether ja/ko use Western or CJK/Hanja numerals (CJK numerals for a countdown read as archaic). This changes the core visual design of the fixed language feature.
issues.source: General Unicode/locale knowledge; corroborated by ICU locale data

issues.claim: The foreground service 'validates that choice' and the fix for screen-off beep failure is to put audio scheduling in the foreground service, decoupled from the Compose/Activity lifecycle.
issues.problem: Necessary but not sufficient. A foreground service does NOT by itself keep the CPU awake through Doze / screen-off; during the silent stretch between intermittent beeps the CPU can sleep and a scheduled beep fires late or not at all — reproducing the exact #1 bug the finding warns about. Also on Android 14+ (target API 36) startForeground() throws MissingForegroundServiceTypeException unless a foregroundServiceType is declared, and there is NO 'timer' type.
issues.correction: Hold a PARTIAL_WAKE_LOCK for the duration of a running session (and, as a sideloaded personal app, exempt it from battery optimization). Declare a foregroundServiceType — realistically specialUse (with android.app.PROPERTY_SPECIAL_USE_FGS_SUBTYPE) or mediaPlayback — plus the matching FOREGROUND_SERVICE_* permission and POST_NOTIFICATIONS (API 33+) runtime permission. Keeping an audio track alive also helps hold the CPU. The drift/reliability self-check must run with the screen actually OFF, not just a fast synthetic loop.

issues.claim: Liquid-glass / frosted-blur surfaces float over the moving gradient (treated as a straightforward given).
issues.problem: Stock Compose Modifier.blur (API 31+) blurs the composable's OWN content, not the backdrop behind it, so it cannot frost the animated gradient sitting under the pause menu. True backdrop blur requires capturing the backdrop via RenderEffect or a third-party library (Haze / Cloudy / Imla), and continuous real-time blur over an always-animating gradient is a genuine GPU/battery cost on a long session.
issues.correction: Budget explicitly for a backdrop-blur approach (name the library/RenderEffect capture) or fake glassmorphism with a translucent surfaceContainer + gradient scrim + border highlight. Do not assume Modifier.blur delivers the glass look.

issues.claim: Scope ducking tightly: request transient (duck) audio focus for exactly the beep's duration and release immediately.
issues.problem: Toggling audio focus five separate times across the final 5 seconds (5s, 3s, 2s, 1s, 0s) makes the user's music dip-restore-dip repeatedly (audible pumping), and some players PAUSE rather than duck on focus loss, so per-beep cycling can stutter or stop their music. 'Independent of media volume' is also only partly achievable — a software gain can boost the sample but cannot exceed the system stream volume.
issues.correction: Consider holding one AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT_MAY_DUCK request across the whole ~5s countdown window rather than per beep; build the AudioFocusRequest with setWillPauseWhenDucked(false); route beeps on a non-media stream (USAGE_ASSISTANCE_SONIFICATION / STREAM_ALARM) so their volume slider is separate; test against players that pause-on-focus-loss.

issues.claim: Specific attributed review quotes, e.g. Gymboss 'stopped beeping when the screen was off', Seconds 'fell behind after multiple intervals', separate in-app volume bar quotes.
issues.problem: Most citations are SEO roundups, review-aggregator scrapers (justuseapp), and product-marketing pages rather than primary sources; the verbatim quotes and their attributions can't be independently verified. The underlying phenomena (screen-off beep failure, quiet beeps under music, end-of-session drift) are real, well-known, and internally consistent, but individual quotes should be treated as illustrative, not verified fact.
issues.correction: Keep the directional conclusions (they are sound and cross-corroborated); do not present the specific quoted complaints as verified evidence in build docs.

additions: Exact platform target: the Galaxy Z Flip 7 ships with Android 16 / One UI 8 = API level 36 (Android 16, 'Baklava', is the current stable release as of mid-2026; Android 17/API 37 is expected later in 2026). Single physical device means minSdk can be set high (34-36) and targetSdk 36. Cover display (FlexWindow) is 4.1", 120Hz, with a camera cutout. Sources: https://www.gsmarena.com/samsung_galaxy_z_flip7-13712.php , https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-galaxy-z-flip7-a-pocket-sized-ai-powerhouse-with-a-new-edge-to-edge-flexwindow

Word mode is a stdlib feature, not custom code: android.icu.text.RuleBasedNumberFormat(locale, RuleBasedNumberFormat.SPELLOUT) spells a number in words per locale (android.icu available API 24+). Do NOT hand-code number words for 13 languages. Caveat to verify at build time: ICU does not ship spellout rules for every locale — confirm coverage for Bengali (bn) and Thai (th) specifically, and check that the default cardinal forms are acceptable (Russian/Arabic have gender/case variants). Source: https://developer.android.com/reference/android/icu/text/RuleBasedNumberFormat

Typography/font coverage is a build blocker the research's Oswald/Anton recommendation misses: a premium bold Latin display face contains NO Devanagari, Bengali, Thai, Arabic-Indic, or CJK glyphs, so the exotic numerals/words will silently fall back to a mismatched system font and break the 'premium' look. Bundle Noto Sans/Serif <script> fonts per language and build a per-language FontFamily. Also: non-Latin digits are not tabular/monospaced, so stabilize the countdown layout with a fixed-size centered container rather than relying on tabular-figures; and handle RTL (Compose LayoutDirection) for Arabic labels.

Perimeter progress stroke on the REAL corners: use WindowInsets.getRoundedCorner(RoundedCorner.POSITION_*) / the RoundedCorner API (API 31+) to read the actual per-corner radius at runtime, draw edge-to-edge (enableEdgeToEdge / WindowCompat.setDecorFitsSystemWindows=false), and route the stroke path around DisplayCutout (the camera hole). The corner radius differs between the folding main display and the 4.1" cover display, so compute it — do not hardcode.

Cover-screen feasibility caveat: there is NO public Samsung API to detect 'I am running on the cover screen' or to ship a dedicated cover layout. Good Lock > MultiStar just launches the normal app on the FlexWindow (an experimental, warranty-safe but Samsung-gated path). Adapt via responsive layout (WindowSizeClass / actual display size) + DisplayCutout, and explicitly verify that the foreground service + audio ducking actually behave when the app is launched through MultiStar, since that path is not a guaranteed/standard Android surface. Sources: https://www.androidcentral.com/phones/samsung-galaxy/these-3-tips-help-me-make-the-most-of-my-samsung-galaxy-z-flip-7-cover-screen

User setup steps that gate the #1 reliability risk (document them, they are not code): because it is a sideloaded no-accounts app, the user must (a) grant the POST_NOTIFICATIONS permission for the foreground-service notification and (b) disable battery optimization for the app — otherwise screen-off beeping can still fail regardless of a correct implementation.

Sequence editor build detail: Jetpack Compose still has no first-party drag-to-reorder for LazyColumn. The insert-between + drag-reorder editor the research (correctly) demands needs a small community helper (e.g. sh.calvin.reorderable) or a manual pointerInput/detectDragGestures implementation — budget for it rather than assuming it is built in.

Beep synthesis API: for precisely-timed synthesized tones that must fire from the service, name a concrete generator — ToneGenerator (simple, stdlib) or a short pre-generated AudioTrack/SoundPool sample (pre-load to avoid first-play latency). SoundPool has load latency, so warm it before the session starts.
confirmedHighlights: Screen-off / backgrounded beep failure is genuinely the category-defining reliability risk, and decoupling audio scheduling from the Compose/Activity lifecycle plus explicitly testing the screen-off case is the correct posture (matches Android FGS guidance) — just pair it with the wake lock / battery-opt fixes noted in the issues.

Color-as-primary-phase-signal (green work / blue rest aura) with one dominant, high-contrast, tabular-figure number sized for ~2 m glance legibility is well-supported and matches the best apps in the market.

Absolute monotonic-clock scheduling — anchor the whole session to elapsedRealtime and compute each boundary as start + cumulative offset rather than chaining off the previous tick — is the correct fix for end-of-session drift.

Tap opens a pause MENU and never one-tap-ends; 'End workout' requiring a second deliberate action is the right guard against accidental floor-reach taps (accidental-pause is a documented, real failure mode).
Editor must support insert-between-any-two + drag-reorder + duplicate + undoable delete — this directly fixes the concrete, verifiable complaint about Seconds' copy/paste-only editor.

Giving the 5s warning tone and the 0s GO tone a timbre distinct from the plain 3-2-1 ticks, and reinforcing the final transition visually (aura peak), correctly mirrors boxing/HIIT audio conventions and adds a non-audio channel when music is loud.

issues.problem: It is an empty placeholder/stub, not research. 'probe', title 't', detail 'd', recommendation 'r' carry zero content. There is nothing to fact-check because no factual, API, or product claim is actually made. As a guide to writing code it is unusable: no SDK levels, no API names, no device facts, no cited sources.
issues.correction: Treat as a non-answer and replace with sourced findings. The verified, build-critical facts an actual build needs are supplied in the additions field below (device specs, target API level, foreground-service type, timing/audio-focus, perimeter-stroke and blur APIs, the 13-language number pipeline, and cover-screen geometry), each with exact API names, minimum SDK levels, and source URLs.

issues.claim: APP SPEC assumption: cover-screen layout must 'keep the bottom-corner camera area clear'.
issues.problem: Sources describe the Z Flip 7 FlexWindow as having a camera cutout at the TOP plus rounded corners (usable area ~95% of the 4.1in rectangle), not necessarily a bottom corner. The physical camera position relative to the app's coordinate space depends on how One UI orients the cover activity, so a hardcoded 'bottom corner' safe-zone is likely wrong and is fragile.
issues.correction: Do not hardcode a corner. Query the real obstructions at runtime: DisplayCutout.getBoundingRects()/getSafeInset* (WindowInsets.getDisplayCutout(), API 28+) for the camera hole, and WindowInsets.getRoundedCorner(position) (API 31+) for each corner radius. Lay the countdown out inside the resulting safe region and set windowLayoutInDisplayCutoutMode = shortEdges. This is also exactly the data the perimeter progress stroke needs.

issues.claim: Implicit build assumption (not stated but the obvious naive path): use Jetpack Compose Modifier.blur for the 'liquid-glass / frosted' surfaces floating over the moving gradient.
issues.problem: Compose's built-in Modifier.blur blurs the composable's OWN pixels, not the content drawn behind it. Applied to a pause-menu surface it will not produce a glassmorphism/backdrop-blur of the moving gradient underneath — the single most-requested visual will silently fail.
issues.correction: Use a backdrop-blur solution: the Haze library (chrisbanes/haze) is the de-facto choice — hazeSource on the gradient background + hazeEffect on the glass surface, with tint. It is built on RenderNode + RenderEffect (API 31+), fine on API 36. skydoves/Cloudy is an alternative. This is the one place a third-party dependency is justified over stdlib.

additions: DEVICE + TARGET SDK (verified): Galaxy Z Flip 7 main display ~6.9in foldable; FlexWindow cover display is 4.1in Super AMOLED, 1048x948 px, up to 120Hz, ~2600 nits. It ships with Android 16 / One UI 8 (launched July 2025), and as of mid-2026 receives One UI 8.x updates still on Android 16. 'Newest Android' therefore = Android 16 = API level 36. Set compileSdk 36 and targetSdk 36; minSdk can safely be 34 or 35 but pinning min=35/36 is fine for a single-device sideload. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Flip_7 , https://www.gsmarena.com/samsung_galaxy_z_flip7-13712.php , https://developer.android.com/about/versions/16/setup-sdk

FOREGROUND SERVICE (verified, load-bearing): From Android 14 (API 34) every foreground service MUST declare a foregroundServiceType in the manifest AND hold the matching runtime permission in addition to FOREGROUND_SERVICE, or startForeground() throws SecurityException. For this timer, 'mediaPlayback' (FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PLAYBACK) is defensible because it emits cued audio, but 'specialUse' (FOREGROUND_SERVICE_SPECIAL_USE) is the honest fit for a timer and — since this is sideloaded with no Play review — avoids the mediaPlayback policy question entirely. Also: the FGS does NOT by itself keep the CPU running with the screen off; hold a PARTIAL_WAKE_LOCK for the duration of an active workout so beeps still fire when the screen is off. And the mandatory FGS notification needs POST_NOTIFICATIONS (runtime permission, API 33+) to be visible — request it. Sources: https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/services/fgs/service-types , https://developer.android.com/about/versions/14/changes/fgs-types-required , https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/views/notifications/notification-permission

TIMING + AUDIO CUES (verified + design nuance): (1) Do not drive the countdown with Handler.postDelayed chains — they accumulate drift. Anchor every cue to SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() (monotonic, unaffected by clock changes) and compute absolute target instants for 5/3/2/1/0. (2) For the beeps use SoundPool with pre-loaded short tone assets (low latency, ideal for repeated short cues) rather than MediaPlayer. (3) Ducking: request AudioManager.requestAudioFocus with AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT_MAY_DUCK and AudioAttributes USAGE_ASSISTANCE_SONIFICATION / CONTENT_TYPE_SONIFICATION; since Android 8 (API 26) the system auto-ducks the other app's music while you hold focus, then restores it when you abandon — exactly 'duck only while the beep sounds.' NUANCE: requesting/abandoning focus on every single 1-second beep can cause audible volume 'pumping.' Prefer holding focus across the whole 5->0 burst (or the ~1s around each tone) and abandoning once, to keep the music dip smooth. Source: https://developer.android.com/media/optimize/audio-focus

PERIMETER PROGRESS STROKE (verified): The rounded-rectangle stroke that traces the display's real corners is directly supported. Use WindowInsets.getRoundedCorner(RoundedCorner.POSITION_TOP_LEFT/TOP_RIGHT/BOTTOM_LEFT/BOTTOM_RIGHT) (API 31+) to get each corner's radius and center, and getDisplayCutout() for the camera hole; build the stroke Path from those exact radii so it hugs the physical corners on BOTH the inner display and the FlexWindow. getRoundedCorner returns null on non-rounded screens/corners, so guard for it. Sources: https://developer.android.com/reference/android/view/RoundedCorner , https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/views/layout/insets/rounded-corners

ANIMATED AURA GRADIENT (verified, with a lazy alternative): A flowing color-shifting field can be done two ways. (a) AGSL RuntimeShader (android.graphics.RuntimeShader, API 33+, fine on 36) applied via Modifier.graphicsLayer { renderEffect = ... } for a true animated shader. (b) MUCH cheaper and usually sufficient: animate the stops/offsets of a Compose Brush.linearGradient / radialGradient with an infinite transition (deep->bright green for work, blue tones for rest) — no shader code, easier to keep at 120Hz on two displays. Recommend starting with (b); reach for AGSL only if the look demands it. Watch GPU cost: a full-screen fragment shader + backdrop blur + 120Hz on the cover panel can drain battery/thermals. Source: https://developer.android.com/reference/android/graphics/RuntimeShader

13-LANGUAGE NUMBERS (verified — this is the biggest sleeper task, and it is mostly free): Android bundles ICU as android.icu.* since API 24, so no dependency is needed. For NATIVE DIGIT GLYPHS use the locale's numbering system (e.g. android.icu.text.NumberFormat / DecimalFormat with the locale, or DecimalFormatSymbols) — Arabic-Indic, Devanagari, Bengali, Thai, and Han digits render automatically. For WORD MODE use android.icu.text.RuleBasedNumberFormat(locale, RuleBasedNumberFormat.SPELLOUT). I verified CLDR/ICU ships spellout rbnf rulesets for bn, th, hi, ar, ru, ko, ja (and en/es/fr/de/pt/zh are long-standing) — https://github.com/unicode-org/cldr/tree/main/common/rbnf . Crucially, word mode only needs cardinals 0-59 ('under a minute'), which every one of these locales covers; and even if any locale's on-device ruleset were incomplete, hardcoding 0-59 in that language is a trivial ~60-word table. FLAG: my directory fetch did not surface zh.xml explicitly (it may have been truncated) — verify Mandarin spellout on the actual device, with the 0-59 hardcode table as the guaranteed fallback. Sources: https://developer.android.com/reference/android/icu/text/RuleBasedNumberFormat , https://developer.android.com/reference/android/icu/text/package-summary

THE 'BYSTANDER CAN'T READ IT' EFFECT HAS A CONTENT GAP (omitted risk): 6 of the 13 languages — English, Spanish, French, German, Portuguese, AND Russian — all use ordinary Western digits 0-9, so in pure DIGIT mode those five/six countdowns look identical to English and are trivially readable. The digit-glyph novelty only actually differs for Han (Chinese/Japanese/Korean share 〇一二三...), Arabic (٠-٩), Devanagari/Hindi (०-९), Bengali (০-৯), and Thai (๐-๙) — about 5 distinct systems. Implication: for the Latin-script + Russian languages the 'intrigue' must come from WORD MODE and the translated 'Work'/'Rest' labels, not digits. Make word-mode prominent (or default) for those locales, and lean on the labels.

FONTS FOR THE 13 SCRIPTS (omitted risk): Do not rely on One UI's system font fallback for Arabic/Devanagari/Bengali/Thai/CJK — silent per-glyph fallback produces inconsistent weights/metrics and undercuts the 'premium' bar. Bundle the display font(s) you actually want (e.g. Noto Sans / Noto Sans Arabic / Devanagari / Bengali / Thai / Noto Sans CJK) as app assets and load via Compose FontFamily, verifying they include the native DIGIT glyphs (not all fonts do) and the 'Work'/'Rest' words. Han unification means one CJK font renders zh/ja/ko word forms with regional glyph differences — pick the per-locale CJK variant (Noto Sans CJK SC/JP/KR) for the labels; the numerals are shared. This is data/asset work to budget for, not a one-liner.

COVER-SCREEN DELIVERY REALITY (verified caveats on the MultiStar path): Running the app on the FlexWindow is done via Good Lock -> MultiStar module -> 'I Heart Galaxy Foldable' -> Launcher Widget, then adding the 'Good Lock Launcher' widget to the cover screen and launching the app from it. Caveats to design around: (1) MultiStar just launches your NORMAL activity on the 4.1in panel — the app must treat 1048x948 as a real configuration and lay out for it (it is NOT a purpose-built cover UI). (2) Good Lock/MultiStar is a user-installed Samsung plugin with regional availability and can change across One UI updates — the cover mode is a 'nice-to-have that depends on a third party,' not a guaranteed platform API. (3) Moving between inner and cover displays is a configuration/display change; make sure the foreground service, wake lock, and audio keep running across it. Sources: https://www.sammobile.com/news/run-any-app-on-galaxy-z-flip-6-flip-7-fe-cover-screen/ , https://www.androidheadlines.com/2025/07/run-any-app-samsung-galaxy-z-flip-7-cover-display-heres-how.html

PRESETS + MISC (low-risk, keep it lazy): Named-JSON presets on device = kotlinx.serialization to app-internal storage (filesDir); no database, no accounts — matches spec. Ladder/pyramid ship as bundled preset JSON, not a generator (spec already says this — good, do not build a generator). targetSdk 36 behavior note: Android 16 forces 'adaptive' layout / ignores orientation+resize locks only on displays with smallest-width >= 600dp; both the Flip's inner phone display and the ~small cover panel are below that threshold, so a portrait lock should still hold — but verify on device. For reliable screen-off operation over long workouts also consider prompting REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS. Source: https://developer.android.com/about/versions/16/behavior-changes-16
confirmedHighlights: Targeting Android 16 / API level 36 as the 'newest Android' is correct and available — the Z Flip 7 ships Android 16 / One UI 8, and Play/tooling already require targetSdk 36 (https://developer.android.com/about/versions/16/setup-sdk).

The cover-screen delivery approach is real and works: Good Lock's MultiStar module can run an arbitrary sideloaded app on the Z Flip 7 FlexWindow via the Good Lock Launcher widget (https://www.sammobile.com/news/run-any-app-on-galaxy-z-flip-6-flip-7-fe-cover-screen/).

Every core visual and audio requirement maps to a real, current API at the target level: perimeter stroke -> RoundedCorner + DisplayCutout (API 31/28), frosted glass -> RenderEffect/Haze (API 31), aura shader -> AGSL RuntimeShader (API 33), beep ducking -> AUDIOFOCUS_GAIN_TRANSIENT_MAY_DUCK (auto-duck since API 26), and 13-language numbers -> bundled android.icu RuleBasedNumberFormat SPELLOUT (API 24). None of the spec's ambitions require anything unavailable on API 36.

research.summary: Build-ready Jetpack Compose guidance for the interval-timer visuals, verified against official Android docs. Target device is the Galaxy Z Flip 7, which ships Android 16 / One UI 8 (API 36), so every API needed here — RuntimeShader (33), Modifier.blur/RenderEffect (31), WindowInsets.getRoundedCorner (31), WindowInsets.displayCutout — is available natively; the sub-API-33 gradient fallback is effectively dead code for a single-device sideload and can be skipped. Key correctness point for the frosted glass: Modifier.blur / graphicsLayer{renderEffect} blur a composable's OWN content, NOT the backdrop behind it — to blur the moving aura behind a floating panel you need either the Haze library (recommended, one modifier, uses RenderEffect on API 31+) or, since you fully own the aura shader, re-draw that shader blurred inside the panel (dependency-free). Continuous animation must be driven by hoisting a time State and reading it INSIDE the draw lambda (drawWithCache/drawBehind) so only the draw phase invalidates, never recomposition.

findings.title: Device/SDK context: Flip 7 is Android 16 (API 36) — every visual API is native, sub-API-33 fallback is dead code
findings.detail: The Galaxy Z Flip 7 ships with Android 16 / One UI 8.0 (updated to One UI 8.5 in May 2026). Main inner display 6.9" 2520x1080 (21:9) with a centered top punch-hole camera; cover 'FlexWindow' 4.1" 1048x948 Super AMOLED, 120Hz, wrapping around the rear dual-camera cluster. Because minSdk can safely be set high for a single-device sideload, ALL APIs in this report are available at runtime: RuntimeShader (API 33), Modifier.blur/RenderEffect (API 31), WindowInsets.getRoundedCorner (API 31), WindowInsets.displayCutout (Compose). PONYTAIL NOTE: the requested 'Brush/gradient fallback below API 33' and 'RenderScript fallback below API 31' are effectively unreachable code on this device — implement the AGSL/RenderEffect paths only and skip the fallbacks unless you later widen device support. Set compileSdk/targetSdk 36. The 120Hz panel means the animated aura must hold a real 120fps budget (see performance finding).

findings.title: (1) Animated aura gradient: AGSL RuntimeShader + ShaderBrush, time uniform via withInfiniteAnimationFrameMillis
(2) Frosted glass BEHIND a panel: Modifier.blur blurs OWN content, not the backdrop — use Haze (recommended) or re-draw the owned shader
findings.detail:
CRITICAL CORRECTNESS POINT: Modifier.blur and graphicsLayer{ renderEffect = RenderEffect.createBlurEffect(rx,ry,CLAMP).asComposeRenderEffect() } (both API 31+, ignored/no-op below 31) blur the composable's OWN rendered content/children — they do NOT have access to and cannot blur what is painted BEHIND the composable in z-order. So you cannot make a pause-menu look like frosted glass over the moving aura with plain Modifier.blur.

Two ways to actually blur the backdrop:
(a) RECOMMENDED — Haze (chrisbanes/haze, Compose Multiplatform). Mark the aura background Modifier.hazeSource(hazeState) and the floating panel Modifier.hazeEffect(hazeState, style){ blurEffect{ blurRadius = 30.dp } } with val hazeState = rememberHazeState(). On Android 12+ (API 31+) Haze uses RenderEffect.createBlurEffect with CLAMP tile mode internally. It captures the source content and re-renders it blurred/tinted under the effect area — exactly the 'liquid glass' look, in ~two modifiers. NOTE the API rename: pre-1.0 used Modifier.haze / Modifier.hazeChild; 1.x+ uses hazeSource / hazeEffect, and 2.x moved blur into a haze-blur module with a blurEffect{} wrapper (dev.chrisbanes.haze.*). Pin the version and use its current docs.
(b) DEPENDENCY-FREE alternative (viable BECAUSE you own the aura shader): inside the panel's own drawBehind, re-draw the same AURA_AGSL ShaderBrush and put a blur RenderEffect on that panel layer (graphicsLayer{ renderEffect = blur }), then layer a translucent white tint (~8-16% alpha) + a thin linear-gradient border highlight on top. This avoids the dependency and the backdrop-capture cost, at the price of the blur being of the gradient only (fine — the gradient IS the whole backdrop). PONYTAIL: if a truly convincing blur isn't essential, the cheapest premium-enough look is skip real blur entirely — translucent dark tint + subtle top-edge white gradient + hairline border reads as 'glass' over the busy aura for a fraction of the GPU cost.
Recommendation: start with (b) for a single fullscreen aura backdrop (no new dependency, you already draw the shader); adopt Haze only if you later layer glass over arbitrary non-shader content.

findings.title: (3) Perimeter progress stroke: rounded-rect Path inset to safe area + PathMeasure.getSegment for a 0..1 partial stroke + glow
(4) Match stroke corner radius to the real display corner via WindowInsets.getRoundedCorner (API 31)
findings.detail:
android.view.WindowInsets.getRoundedCorner(position) returns a RoundedCorner (API 31+) with getRadius() (px) and getCenter() (Point). Positions: RoundedCorner.POSITION_TOP_LEFT / TOP_RIGHT / BOTTOM_LEFT / BOTTOM_RIGHT. Returns null if there is no rounded corner or it falls outside the app's window bounds (e.g. emulator, or app not fullscreen).

In Compose, reach the platform insets via LocalView.current.rootWindowInsets (or the Activity's decorView):
val view = LocalView.current
val radiusPx = remember {
  view.rootWindowInsets?.getRoundedCorner(RoundedCorner.POSITION_TOP_LEFT)?.radius?.toFloat() ?: (28.dp).value // fallback
}
Use that radius for the CornerRadius in the perimeter path so the stroke follows the display's real corners. ALWAYS keep a sensible dp fallback (the Flip 7's actual radius is not published — read it at runtime, don't hardcode). Corners can differ per position; for a symmetric stroke use the max of the four, or read all four if you want per-corner accuracy. rootWindowInsets may be null before the view is attached — read it after first layout (remember keyed on the view, or in a LaunchedEffect).

findings.title: (5) Keep the stroke/content clear of the camera via WindowInsets.displayCutout / DisplayCutout bounding rects
findings.detail: Compose: WindowInsets.displayCutout gives the inset region occupied by cutouts; WindowInsets.safeDrawing already folds displayCutout together with system-bar insets and is the usual choice to pad content. For the exact camera rectangle (to route the perimeter stroke and big countdown around it), get the platform DisplayCutout: view.rootWindowInsets.displayCutout, then DisplayCutout.boundingRects (List<Rect>) or getBoundingRectTop()/Left()/Right()/Bottom(); DisplayCutout also exposes safeInsetTop/Left/Right/Bottom, and Compose exposes WindowInsets.displayCutout with a cutoutPath. On the MAIN inner screen the Flip 7 has a centered top punch-hole, so the top run of the perimeter stroke should be inset below safeInsetTop and the countdown must avoid the top-center rect. For the COVER FlexWindow, the app spec says keep the bottom-corner camera area clear — do NOT hardcode that geometry; read the actual cutout/safe insets at runtime (they differ between the two displays and across One UI updates) and inset the stroke + layout to the returned safe region. Enable edge-to-edge (WindowCompat.setDecorFitsSystemWindows(window,false) / enableEdgeToEdge()) and set the cutout mode to shortEdges or 'always' so you're allowed to draw into the cutout region and can then carve around it yourself.

findings.title: (6) Performance: keep continuous animation in the DRAW phase, never recomposition
findings.detail:
The aura, aura-blur, and perimeter stroke all animate every frame at up to 120Hz, so the hard rule is: do NOT let per-frame values trigger recomposition or relayout. Techniques (all official Compose guidance):
- Drive frame time with produceState + withInfiniteAnimationFrameMillis, and READ the resulting State.value INSIDE the draw lambda (onDrawBehind / drawBehind / graphicsLayer block). A state read inside a draw lambda invalidates only the draw phase — recomposition and layout are skipped. Reading the same State at the composable's top level would recompose every frame — avoid.
- Create expensive objects (RuntimeShader, Path, PathMeasure, Brush) ONCE in Modifier.drawWithCache; it re-runs only when size or captured keys change, not per frame.
- Prefer drawBehind over a Canvas() composable for pure background painting (fewer nodes). Use graphicsLayer for the blur/glow layers so the blur composites on RenderThread.
- Modifier.blur / RenderEffect blur over a large, constantly-repainting surface is the single most expensive item here — apply it to the smallest region possible (the glass panel, not the whole screen) and to a cached/less-frequently-updated layer where you can. If the aura already animates, a separately-blurred full-screen copy doubles GPU cost; the 'own-shader re-draw' glass approach (finding 2b) or a static-tint glass keeps the budget.
- Cross-interval color changes: animate uniform colors with animateColorAsState and feed them as uniforms in the draw lambda rather than recomposing the shader.
- Watch the AGSL cost: keep the shader's per-pixel math cheap (a few sin/cos, no loops) since it runs on every pixel of a 2520x1080 panel at 120Hz. Profile with the Layout Inspector recomposition counts (should stay flat while animating) and GPU rendering profiler.

recommendations: Set compileSdk/targetSdk = 36 and a high minSdk; implement only the AGSL (API 33) and RenderEffect (API 31) paths and SKIP the sub-API-33 gradient / sub-API-31 RenderScript fallbacks — they are unreachable on the Flip 7's Android 16 and are pure over-engineering for a single-device sideload.

Aura background: RuntimeShader + ShaderBrush created once in Modifier.drawWithCache; drive time via produceState+withInfiniteAnimationFrameMillis and read the time/progress/color State INSIDE onDrawBehind so only the draw phase invalidates. Feed a 0..1 iProgress uniform for deep->bright and cross-fade green/blue color uniforms with animateColorAsState on work/rest transitions.

Frosted glass: do NOT expect Modifier.blur/graphicsLayer renderEffect to blur the backdrop — they blur the composable's own content. Default to the dependency-free approach: re-draw the owned aura ShaderBrush blurred inside the pause panel + translucent tint + hairline gradient border. Reach for the Haze library (hazeSource/hazeEffect, RenderEffect on API 31+) only if you later need to blur non-shader content.

Perimeter stroke: build one closed RoundRect Path inset to the safe region, measure with Compose PathMeasure, and use getSegment(0f, length*progress, dst) each frame (rewind dst first). Add glow with a second wide low-alpha stroke on a blurred graphicsLayer rather than a CPU BlurMaskFilter.

Corner radius + cutout: read them at runtime — WindowInsets.getRoundedCorner(POSITION_*) for the corner radius and view.rootWindowInsets.displayCutout / WindowInsets.displayCutout for the camera rect — with dp fallbacks. Never hardcode the Flip 7's corner radius or the cover-screen camera geometry; they aren't published and differ per display. Enable edge-to-edge + shortEdges cutout mode.

Hold a 120Hz budget: keep AGSL per-pixel math cheap, cache shader/path/pathmeasure in drawWithCache, confine any real blur to the smallest region, and verify recomposition counts stay flat while animating.
gotchas: Modifier.blur and graphicsLayer{renderEffect=BlurEffect} blur the composable's OWN content, not what is drawn behind it in z-order — a common misconception that will make a naive 'frosted panel over the aura' look wrong. Backdrop blur requires Haze or re-drawing the owned backdrop.

Modifier.blur / RenderEffect are no-ops below API 31 and RuntimeShader throws below API 33 — irrelevant on the Flip 7 (Android 16) but will crash/blank on older test emulators, so guard with @RequiresApi or a min-API emulator image when testing.

WindowInsets.getRoundedCorner and rootWindowInsets.displayCutout can return null (before the view is attached, on emulators, or when the feature isn't present) — always provide a dp fallback and read after first layout.

Compose PathMeasure historically had a getSegment caching bug requiring setPath to be re-called; rewind() the destination Path every frame and re-run setPath whenever the source path (size/inset/radius) changes.

Haze changed its public API across versions: pre-1.0 haze/hazeChild -> 1.x hazeSource/hazeEffect -> 2.x split blur into a haze-blur module with a blurEffect{} wrapper (dev.chrisbanes.haze.*). Pin a version and follow that version's docs; older tutorials will not compile.

The official AGSL animation sample drives the time uniform with a Views ValueAnimator, not Compose — port it to produceState+withInfiniteAnimationFrameMillis for Compose, and read the value in the draw phase to avoid per-frame recomposition.
openQuestions: The Flip 7's exact display corner radius and the cover-screen (FlexWindow) camera cutout geometry are not published by Samsung and the cover screen wraps around the rear cameras rather than having a standard punch-hole — these MUST be read at runtime via WindowInsets APIs; confirm on-device that getRoundedCorner and displayCutout return non-null useful values on BOTH the inner and cover displays.

Running the full-screen Compose UI on the cover 'FlexWindow' requires Good Lock 'MultiStar' (Launch widget / cover-screen enablement); whether WindowInsets.displayCutout / getRoundedCorner report correct values in that MultiStar-hosted context (vs. the normal inner-display Activity) needs on-device verification — this is a separate cover-screen dimension but directly affects where the perimeter stroke and countdown can safely draw.

Whether a fully real backdrop blur (Haze) is worth its GPU cost at 120Hz over the already-animating aura, versus the dependency-free re-drawn-shader-glass or a static translucent tint — decide by profiling on the actual device.

confirmedHighlights: Device/SDK: Galaxy Z Flip 7 shipped Android 16 / One UI 8 out of the box (the FIRST devices to do so, with the Fold 7), so compileSdk/targetSdk 36 and the 'all APIs native, fallbacks are dead code' conclusion is correct. Main display 6.9in 2520x1080 21:9 Dynamic AMOLED 2X (1-120Hz); cover FlexWindow 4.1in 1048x948 Super AMOLED up to 120Hz. All specs verified. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Flip_7 , https://9to5google.com/2025/07/07/galaxy-z-fold-7-flip-7-reportedly-launching-with-android-16/ , https://www.gsmarena.com/samsung_galaxy_z_flip7-13712.php

SDK version gates all correct: RuntimeShader = API 33 (Android 13/Tiramisu); RenderEffect / RenderEffect.createBlurEffect(rx,ry,TileMode) / Modifier.blur = API 31 (Android 12); WindowInsets.getRoundedCorner + RoundedCorner.POSITION_* = API 31. Sources: https://developer.android.com/reference/android/graphics/RuntimeShader , https://developer.android.com/reference/android/graphics/RenderEffect , https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/views/layout/insets/rounded-corners

CENTRAL CORRECTNESS CLAIM IS RIGHT: Modifier.blur and graphicsLayer{renderEffect=blur} blur the composable's OWN content, not the z-order backdrop behind it. Backdrop blur genuinely requires Haze (which captures the source via hazeSource/hazeEffect) or re-drawing the owned shader. This is the most valuable and most-often-gotten-wrong point in the doc and it is accurate.

API names are real and correctly packaged (no hallucinations): withInfiniteAnimationFrameMillis (androidx.compose.animation.core), ShaderBrush, RuntimeShader.setFloatUniform/setColorUniform, produceState, drawWithCache/onDrawBehind, animateColorAsState, DisplayCutout.boundingRects/getSafeInsetTop, RoundedCorner.getRadius/getCenter.

Compose PathMeasure signatures verified exactly: getSegment(startDistance: Float, stopDistance: Float, destination: Path, startWithMoveTo: Boolean = true): Boolean, and setPath(path: Path?, forceClosed: Boolean), plus the length property. Source: https://developer.android.com/reference/kotlin/androidx/compose/ui/graphics/PathMeasure

Haze 2.0 architecture claim is directionally correct: pre-1.0 haze/hazeChild -> 1.x hazeSource/hazeEffect -> 2.x uses a blurEffect{} wrapper inside hazeEffect. Source: https://chrisbanes.me/posts/haze-2.0/ , https://chrisbanes.github.io/haze/latest/migrating-2.0/

issues.claim: 'The Galaxy Z Flip 7 ships with Android 16 / One UI 8.0 (updated to One UI 8.5 in May 2026).'
issues.problem: As of May 2026 One UI 8.5 (Android 16-based) was still in BETA on the Fold 7 / Flip 7 with the stable rollout explicitly delayed, not a completed update. Stating it as 'updated to One UI 8.5 in May 2026' overstates the status. Low impact on the build (every API needed is in the Android 16 base that shipped July 2025), but the factual claim is imprecise.
issues.correction: Flip 7 shipped July 2025 on Android 16 / One UI 8.0; One UI 8.5 (still Android 16-based, so no new API surface for this app) was in beta around May 2026 with stable rollout taking time. None of it changes the API set.

issues.claim: Haze 2.x 'moved blur into a haze-blur module with a blurEffect{} wrapper (dev.chrisbanes.haze.*).'
issues.problem: Imprecise in a build-relevant way. In Haze 2.x the blur APIs live in the dev.chrisbanes.haze.blur package and ship in a SEPARATE gradle module (dev.chrisbanes.haze:haze-blur); the core dev.chrisbanes.haze:haze module no longer contains the blur effect. If you add only the core 'haze' dependency you will not have blurEffect{} and it won't compile.
issues.correction: For the recommended Haze path on 2.x, depend on BOTH dev.chrisbanes.haze:haze (core: rememberHazeState, hazeSource, hazeEffect) and dev.chrisbanes.haze:haze-blur (the blurEffect{} wrapper + HazeColorEffect.tint, in package dev.chrisbanes.haze.blur; materials in dev.chrisbanes.haze.blur.materials). Pin the version.

issues.claim: '...and Compose exposes WindowInsets.displayCutout with a cutoutPath.'
issues.problem: Conflates two different APIs. Compose's WindowInsets.displayCutout is only an inset REGION (top/left/right/bottom padding); it does not expose a cutout Path. The actual cutout outline Path comes from the platform DisplayCutout.getCutoutPath() (added API 31), reached via view.rootWindowInsets.displayCutout.
issues.correction: Use WindowInsets.displayCutout / WindowInsets.safeDrawing (Compose) for padding, and DisplayCutout.getBoundingRects()/getSafeInsetTop() or getCutoutPath() (platform, API 31) for the exact camera geometry to route the stroke around. There is no 'cutoutPath' on the Compose WindowInsets object.

additions: Dependency-free glass (finding 2b) has an unstated coordinate-space trap: to make the re-drawn AURA_AGSL shader inside the pause panel actually read as the backdrop 'showing through', the shader must be evaluated in SCREEN coordinates (same iResolution = full display size, and fragCoord offset by the panel's top-left position on screen), not the panel's local coordinate space. If you naively draw the same brush inside the panel it renders a mismatched mini-gradient that doesn't line up with the aura behind it, breaking the illusion. Pass the panel's onGloballyPositioned offset into the shader (or an iPanelOffset uniform) so the re-draw is continuous with the background. Haze avoids this because it captures the real source pixels.

enableEdgeToEdge vs setDecorFitsSystemWindows: the doc lists WindowCompat.setDecorFitsSystemWindows(window,false) as an option, but that call is deprecated; prefer Activity.enableEdgeToEdge() (androidx.activity). Also note that on targetSdk 35+ (this app is 36) edge-to-edge is ENFORCED by default, so you get it for free and mainly need to handle insets/cutout yourself. Source: https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/views/layout/edge-to-edge

The 'Compose PathMeasure getSegment caching bug requiring setPath re-call' is stated as historical fact but I could not confirm a specific tracker issue for the Compose (androidx.compose.ui.graphics) PathMeasure. The advice (rewind() the destination each frame; re-run setPath when the source path changes, which drawWithCache does on size change) is harmless and correct defensive practice regardless. Treat the specific 'bug' as unverified folklore, not a documented defect.

Animation driver detail worth stating explicitly for the foreground-service spec: withInfiniteAnimationFrameMillis is driven by the Compose frame clock, which STOPS when the screen is off / app not composed. That is correct and desirable for the VISUALS (no point rendering the aura to a dark screen, saves battery), but it means the timer/beep logic must be driven by the foreground service's own wall clock (SystemClock.elapsedRealtime), NOT by the animation frame count. The doc's performance section is right that reads belong in the draw phase; just don't let the visual clock also be the source of truth for interval timing.

Cover-screen (FlexWindow) reality check to add to the open question: Samsung's cover display normally only runs a whitelisted set of apps; Good Lock 'MultiStar' (Launch widget / 'I love Galaxy Foldable' > cover-screen app enablement) is what lets an arbitrary sideloaded Activity run there, and the app runs in a constrained, non-standard window. Whether getRoundedCorner()/rootWindowInsets.displayCutout report correct values in that MultiStar-hosted context is genuinely uncertain and MUST be verified on-device — the doc flags this correctly; just be prepared for the APIs to return null/wrong values on the cover screen and keep the runtime-read + dp-fallback path mandatory there.

research.summary: Verified Samsung Galaxy Z Flip 7 (2025) hardware and Android-API facts for rendering the interval timer on both the cover (FlexWindow) and inner displays. Cover display is a 4.1" Super AMOLED, 1048x948 px, ~345 ppi, near-square, 120Hz, with rounded corners and the dual rear cameras cutting into its lower-left region. Device ships Android 16 / One UI 8 (API level 36). Running an arbitrary app on the cover screen is unofficial: it requires Good Lock + the MultiStar module's Launcher Widget, and MultiStar (not the app) controls whether the app gets the full panel, an area above the cameras, or a letterboxed mini view. Key correction: there is NO public Display.FLAG_REAR constant; cover-vs-inner detection must come from live WindowMetrics/Display name plus runtime WindowInsets queries for the cutout and rounded corners, not a hard-coded flag. Several precise geometry numbers (exact camera-cutout pixel rect, cover-display dp/density, cover-face screen-to-body %) are NOT published by Samsung and must be measured on-device.

findings.title: Cover (FlexWindow) display core specs: 4.1", 1048x948 px, ~345 ppi, near-square, 120Hz
findings.detail: Cover display is 4.1 inches, Super AMOLED, resolution 1048 x 948 px (Samsung/Wikipedia list it 1048x948 portrait; GSMArena writes 948x1048 — same panel), up to 120Hz, 2600 nits peak, Gorilla Glass Victus 2. Aspect ratio ~1.105:1 tall (i.e. ~0.905:1 width:height) — essentially near-square, marginally taller than wide (~9:10). Pixel density is NOT officially published; calculated sqrt(948^2+1048^2)/4.1 = ~345 ppi (approximate — 4.1" is a nominal diagonal, panel is non-rectangular). Do NOT hard-code dp: read DisplayMetrics/WindowMetrics at runtime; the cover density bucket and dp size are undocumented and differ from the inner display. YesViz documents only the inner display (360x840 dp, DPR 3), not the cover.

findings.title: Cover display shape: rounded corners + dual cameras cutting into lower-left; exact cutout rect NOT published
findings.detail: The 4.1" FlexWindow spans edge-to-edge with ~1.25mm bezels and physically WRAPS AROUND the two rear camera lenses (plus LED flash), which sit in the lower-left region when the FlexWindow is viewed upright (hinge at top) — matching the spec's 'keep the bottom-corner camera area clear.' Samsung notes the viewable area is ~95% of the full rectangle due to rounded corners and the lower camera cutout. UNCERTAIN: Samsung does not publish corner radius or exact camera-cutout coordinates/shape, and it is unclear whether the cameras are exposed to apps as a true DisplayCutout or simply sit outside a rounded-rectangle panel. MultiStar's 'stop app UI extending below the cameras' toggle implies the usable region CAN extend down around the cameras and they interrupt the lower area. Guidance: query WindowInsets.getDisplayCutout(), getRoundedCorner(pos), getDisplayShape() at runtime; if the cover returns an empty cutout, fall back to keeping the bottom-left corner (~bottom 15-20%) clear and expose a calibration offset measured on the physical device.

findings.title: Inner display (reference): 6.9", 2520x1080 px, 21:9, ~397 ppi, 1-120Hz LTPO
findings.detail: Main foldable inner display: 6.9 inches, Dynamic/LTPO AMOLED 2X, 2520x1080 px, 21:9, ~397 ppi, adaptive 1-120Hz, 2600 nits peak. In dp: 360x840 at density 3.0 (xxhdpi/DPR 3) per YesViz. Body: unfolded 166.7 x 75.2 x 6.5 mm; folded 85.5 x 75.2 x 13.7 mm; 188 g. Inner selfie camera is a centered top punch-hole (10 MP). This is the surface the app renders on when unfolded.

findings.title: Ships Android 16 / One UI 8, Exynos 2500 -> target API level 36
findings.detail: The Z Flip 7 ships with Android 16 and One UI 8.0 (later One UI 8.5), SoC Exynos 2500 (3nm). Android 16 = API level 36, so compileSdk/targetSdk = 36 and minSdk can also be 36 for this single-device build. All newest display APIs (DisplayShape/getShape API 34, getRoundedCorner API 31, getDisplayCutout API 28) are available with no compat shims.

findings.title: Cover-screen app deployment: unofficial, requires Good Lock + MultiStar Launcher Widget; MultiStar controls sizing
findings.detail: No official Android/Samsung path launches an arbitrary third-party app on the FlexWindow. Working method: (1) install Good Lock (Galaxy Store), (2) install the MultiStar module, (3) MultiStar > 'I heart Galaxy Foldable' > 'Launcher Widget', select up to ~12 apps, (4) Settings > Cover screen > Widgets, add the 'Good Lock Launcher' widget to the cover carousel, (5) fold, swipe to the launcher widget, tap the app. Apps do NOT get raw full-display privileges — MultiStar sandboxes them and offers per-app display modes: full screen, an area ABOVE the cameras, or a small vertical 'mini' view, plus a button to stop UI extending below the camera line. Implication: the timer cannot assume it owns the full cover panel; it must be robust to a reduced/letterboxed area and size everything off live window bounds. Biggest deployment risk — verify the actual usable rectangle on the physical device early.

findings.title: CORRECTION: no public Display.FLAG_REAR; detect cover-vs-inner from WindowMetrics/Display name, not a flag
findings.detail: There is NO public Display.FLAG_REAR. The API 35 Display class publishes only FLAG_PRESENTATION, FLAG_PRIVATE, FLAG_ROUND, FLAG_SECURE, FLAG_SUPPORTS_PROTECTED_BUFFERS (FLAG_REAR exists only as a hidden AOSP constant). Public detection signals: (a) DisplayManager.getDisplays() to enumerate; Display.getDisplayId(), Display.getName() (Samsung foldables usually name the cover panel distinctively — confirm the exact string on-device); (b) Activity.getDisplay() (API 30+) for the active display; (c) most robust and recommended: WindowManager.getCurrentWindowMetrics().getBounds() (or WindowMetricsCalculator) and branch on size — cover is near-square/small (~948x1048), inner is tall 21:9 (~1080x2520). On Flip devices cover/inner behave as a swapping default display, so the size signal reacts correctly via onConfigurationChanged. Do not hard-code 'am I on the cover' — drive the whole layout off live WindowMetrics + WindowInsets.

findings.title: Runtime APIs for cutout + rounded corners + display shape, with min SDK levels
findings.detail: To compute the camera-clear region and perimeter-stroke path from real hardware at runtime: WindowInsets.getDisplayCutout() (min API 28) returns DisplayCutout with getBoundingRects()/getSafeInset*; DisplayCutout.getCutoutPath() is API 31+. WindowInsets.getRoundedCorner(int position) and RoundedCorner (getRadius/getCenter) are min API 31 (also Display.getRoundedCorner). Display.getShape() -> DisplayShape and WindowInsets.getDisplayShape() (returns a Path of the actual physical display outline — ideal for tracing the real rounded-rectangle perimeter) are min API 34. All available on Android 16. For the perimeter progress stroke, getDisplayShape().getPath() is the correct source for true corner geometry rather than guessing a radius. Caveat: whether the cover display reports a cutout/shape for the cameras is unverified — test on the physical unit and keep a manual calibration fallback.

findings.title: Jetpack WindowManager for posture; WindowAreaController Rear Display Mode is a different (unfolded) use case
findings.detail: Jetpack WindowManager (androidx.window) is stable at 1.5 (Oct 2025); 1.4+ adds richer foldable info. WindowInfoTracker.getOrCreate(context).windowLayoutInfo(...) emits FoldingFeature (state FLAT/HALF_OPENED, orientation, occlusion) for posture-aware layout. NOTE: posture alone does NOT distinguish cover-vs-inner when the phone is closed on the FlexWindow — combine it with the WindowMetrics size signal. Separately, WindowManager's Rear Display Mode (WindowAreaController / WindowAreaSession, androidx.window 1.2+) can move an activity to the outer screen, but it targets the UNFOLDED selfie/preview scenario (inner display turns off) and is NOT the mechanism for a folded MultiStar-launched cover app — context only; MultiStar remains the deployment path.

recommendations: Build ONE responsive Compose layout driven entirely by live WindowManager.getCurrentWindowMetrics() bounds + WindowInsets, not two hard-coded layouts. This automatically handles inner display, cover display, and whatever cropped rectangle MultiStar grants — and it is less code than branching on a display flag that does not publicly exist.

Trace the perimeter progress stroke from WindowInsets.getDisplayShape().getPath() (API 34+) so it follows the display's real rounded corners instead of an assumed radius. Keep a manual corner-radius/inset calibration constant as a fallback for the cover screen, whose shape reporting is unverified.

For the camera-clear zone, read WindowInsets.getDisplayCutout() first; if the cover reports no cutout, fall back to a configurable bottom-left keep-out rectangle and TUNE it on the physical device. Leave it as an adjustable value, not a magic number baked into the render path.

Validate the MultiStar deployment path on the actual phone before investing in cover-screen polish: install Good Lock + MultiStar, add the app to the Launcher Widget, and record the exact usable pixel rectangle plus which display mode (full / above-cameras / mini) yields a clean full-bleed surface. Everything downstream depends on that measured rectangle.
Set compileSdk/targetSdk 36 (Android 16); minSdk 36 is fine for this single-device build and unlocks getDisplayShape/getRoundedCorner/getCutout with no compat code.

Verify foreground-service beeps and background-music ducking keep working while the app runs on the cover screen with the FlexWindow off — this is untested for MultiStar-hosted apps and is core to the app's purpose.
gotchas: Display.FLAG_REAR is NOT public API — do not detect the cover screen with it; use WindowMetrics size + Display.getName() instead.
MultiStar, not your app, decides the cover-screen window size and can letterbox or clip it; the app cannot assume it owns the full 1048x948 panel.

Exact cover-screen camera-cutout coordinates, corner radius, cover dp/density, and cover-face screen-to-body % are NOT published by Samsung; treat any such number as measure-on-device, not spec-derived.
Resolution is written both 1048x948 (Samsung/Wikipedia, portrait) and 948x1048 (GSMArena) — same panel; be explicit about orientation in code.

Whether the cover display reports the cameras via getDisplayCutout()/getDisplayShape() is unverified; the panel may present as a clean rounded rectangle with the cameras physically outside it, making cutout queries return empty on the cover.

A foreground service is needed for screen-off timing/beeps, but cover-screen (folded, screen-off) doze/power behavior for MultiStar-hosted apps is untested — verify beeps continue when the FlexWindow times out.

Notably the 2600-nit figure — which I expected might be inner-only — is confirmed for the COVER display too. Source: https://www.gsmarena.com/samsung_galaxy_z_flip7-13712.php

Body/SoC correct: unfolded 166.7x75.2x6.5mm, folded 85.5x75.2x13.7mm, 188g, Exynos 2500 (3nm, Xclipse 950 GPU). Source: GSMArena.

KEY CORRECTION IS CORRECT: Display.FLAG_REAR is @hide in AOSP (public static final int FLAG_REAR = 1<<13, annotated @hide) and NOT in the public SDK. The five public Display flags listed (FLAG_PRESENTATION, FLAG_PRIVATE, FLAG_ROUND, FLAG_SECURE, FLAG_SUPPORTS_PROTECTED_BUFFERS) are exactly the public set. Verified against AOSP core/java/android/view/Display.java. The recommendation to branch on WindowMetrics/Display.getName() instead is sound.

All display APIs verified real with correct SDK gates: DisplayCutout (API 28), DisplayCutout.getCutoutPath()/getBoundingRects()/getSafeInset* (getCutoutPath API 31), WindowInsets.getRoundedCorner(int)+RoundedCorner+Display.getRoundedCorner (API 31), Display.getShape()->DisplayShape and WindowInsets.getDisplayShape() (API 34). Verified against developer.android.com and the dotnet/android-api-docs mirror (ApiSince tags: DisplayCutout=28, DisplayShape=34).

Jetpack WindowManager version claim correct: androidx.window 1.5.0 went stable Oct 2025; WindowInfoTracker/FoldingFeature (FLAT/HALF_OPENED) and WindowAreaController Rear Display Mode (1.2+, an unfolded-selfie use case, NOT the folded MultiStar path) are all accurately characterized. Source: https://developer.android.com/blog/posts/jetpack-window-manager-1-5-is-stable

A beep/timer with audio has no clean category — closest is mediaPlayback (FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PLAYBACK); FOREGROUND_SERVICE_SPECIAL_USE is the honest fallback (Play scrutiny is irrelevant here since it's sideloaded). This is OS-enforced, not Play-enforced. The JSON raises 'verify FGS beeps work' but never names the type/permission requirement. Source: https://developer.android.com/develop/background-work/services/fgs/service-types

OMISSION for the perimeter-stroke feature specifically: getDisplayShape().getPath() gives the corner geometry, but to actually RENDER the stroke out to the physical edges/corners the window must go edge-to-edge and be allowed into the cutout region — WindowCompat.setDecorFitsSystemWindows(window,false) / enableEdgeToEdge(), plus window.attributes.layoutInDisplayCutoutMode = LAYOUT_IN_DISPLAY_CUTOUT_MODE_ALWAYS (ALWAYS added API 30). On targetSdk 35+ edge-to-edge is already default-enforced, so this is mostly the cutout-mode line plus reading insets to keep the camera keep-out clear. Worth stating alongside the getDisplayShape recommendation. Source: https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/views/layout/edge-to-edge and https://developer.android.com/reference/android/view/WindowManager.LayoutParams#LAYOUT_IN_DISPLAY_CUTOUT_MODE_ALWAYS
